title: Mould & Indoor Air Quality Investigation
short: Find the moisture source driving the mould, with NATA-accredited laboratory analysis behind the finding.
headline: Killing the mould without finding the water just buys you six months.
intro: Mould is a symptom. Something is keeping a surface wet for long enough to let it establish, and unless that source is identified the growth returns after remediation. A BEWG investigation identifies the moisture mechanism first, then quantifies the indoor air quality impact through sampling analysed by a NATA-accredited laboratory.
signs: Visible growth returning in the same place after cleaning or remediation
A persistent musty smell with no visible growth to explain it
Occupants reporting respiratory symptoms, headaches or fatigue that ease when they leave the building
A remediation contractor recommending works without a documented moisture source
An insurer or strata manager requesting independent verification before approving scope
method: Site walkthrough and occupant history to establish onset, seasonality and affected zones
Moisture mapping of affected and adjacent areas to trace the water back to its source
Psychrometric readings to establish whether condensation is forming, and where
Air and surface sampling where the exposure question needs answering, analysed by a NATA-accredited laboratory
Interpretation of laboratory results against occupancy, ventilation and the moisture findings
deliverables: Identified moisture source and the mechanism keeping it wet
Laboratory analysis with interpretation, not just raw counts
Photographic record with moisture readings tied to locations
Remediation scope written so a contractor can price it and an insurer can assess it
Clearance criteria defining what completion actually looks like

title: Moisture Mapping & 3D Moisture Mapping
short: Map the true extent of water through a building, including multi-storey and major loss, before anyone opens a wall.
headline: The wet area is almost never the size it looks.
intro: Water travels. It runs along framing, tracks under floor coverings and drops through slab penetrations into levels nobody has inspected. Moisture mapping records the actual extent as measured data across a floor plan, so demolition scope, drying strategy and claim value rest on evidence instead of estimate. For multi-storey and major loss events the mapping is built in three dimensions, following the water between levels.
signs: A burst pipe, storm event or flood where the affected area is not yet defined
Water on an upper level with unknown migration into levels below
A strata dispute over which lots and common property are affected
A drying contractor and an assessor disagreeing on scope
Damage suspected behind finishes that nobody wants to open speculatively
method: Non-invasive scanning across affected and adjacent areas to establish boundaries
Invasive metering at calibrated depths to confirm what the non-invasive readings suggest
Thermal imaging to reveal evaporative cooling patterns and thermal anomalies
Level-by-level mapping for multi-storey losses, tracing migration paths vertically
Readings plotted onto floor plans as a measured record, with reference readings from dry areas
deliverables: Floor plans marked with moisture readings and mapped affected boundaries
Three-dimensional migration path for multi-storey and major loss events
Thermal imagery paired with the meter readings that confirm it
Defined demolition and drying scope tied to measured data
Baseline for monitoring drying progress and verifying completion
standards: IICRC S500 water damage restoration principles

title: Condensation & Interstitial Moisture Diagnosis
short: Establish whether the water is coming in from outside or forming inside, and fix the right problem.
headline: Half the leaks we are called to investigate are not leaks.
intro: Condensation and water ingress present almost identically: staining, mould, damp smell, deteriorating finishes. The rectification for each is completely different, and treating one as the other wastes the entire budget. This investigation separates them using psychrometric measurement and thermal analysis, and where the moisture is forming inside the wall rather than on it, identifies the interface where it is accumulating.
signs: Damp that appears in winter and improves in summer
Mould on cold surfaces such as window reveals, external corners and behind furniture
A building that has become damp since windows, insulation or heating were upgraded
Water damage with no identifiable leak after plumbing has been checked
Recurring damp in a bathroom, laundry or kitchen with poor or ducted-to-nowhere ventilation
method: Psychrometric readings across affected zones, establishing dew point against measured surface temperatures
Thermal imaging to locate thermal bridging and cold spots where condensation forms first
Ventilation assessment, including whether exhaust fans discharge outside the building
Carbon dioxide measurement as an indicator of actual air change rate under occupancy
Envelope review to identify vapour control layer position and insulation continuity
deliverables: Clear determination of ingress, condensation or both, with the measurement supporting it
The specific surfaces and interfaces where condensation is occurring and why
Ventilation adequacy assessment against actual occupancy
Rectification options separated into ventilation, heating, insulation and envelope work
Where relevant, referral to hygrothermal modelling for assembly-level analysis

title: Hygrothermal Modelling
short: Model condensation risk inside a wall assembly at design stage, before it is built and before the callbacks.
headline: An assembly can meet every prescriptive requirement and still grow mould in two winters.
intro: NCC prescriptive compliance does not assess interstitial condensation risk. Hygrothermal modelling simulates heat and moisture movement through a wall, roof or floor assembly under real hourly climate data for the specific project location, showing where moisture accumulates, whether condensation forms at critical interfaces, and whether the assembly can dry out between seasons. Engaged during design development it redirects a specification. Engaged after construction it confirms a problem that is now expensive.
signs: A highly insulated assembly being specified for a cooler or more humid climate than it has been used in before
Uncertainty about which side of the insulation the vapour control layer belongs on
A certifier or client requiring condensation risk verification
A wall type that has performed on previous projects being reused in a different climate zone
Existing buildings where condensation is suspected inside the assembly rather than on its surface
method: Assembly definition layer by layer, with material properties assigned from referenced data
Climate data selected for the specific project location rather than a generic climate zone
Simulation across multiple years to capture seasonal accumulation and drying behaviour
Assessment of moisture content and relative humidity at each material interface
Where the assembly fails, modelling of the revised design to confirm the fix works
deliverables: Moisture and temperature profile at every layer across a full annual cycle
Identification of the critical interface and the severity of condensation risk there
Mould growth index at critical interfaces against accepted thresholds
Specific design modification where the assembly fails, with the revised model included
Documentation structured for submission to certifiers and building surveyors
standards: NCC Section J and condensation management
Bureau of Meteorology hourly climate data

title: Building Defect & Water Ingress Investigation
short: Establish the mechanism of failure and who is responsible, with evidence that holds up in a dispute.
headline: Knowing the building leaks is not the finding. Knowing why is.
intro: Most building defects are not visible at the surface, and the visible damage rarely sits where the failure is. A defect investigation reverse engineers the failure: establishing the path water is taking, identifying whether the cause is design, materials or workmanship, and documenting it to a standard that survives scrutiny from the other side.
signs: Water ingress through a facade, window, balcony or roof that previous repairs have not resolved
A defects claim during the statutory warranty period
Strata common property water ingress affecting multiple lots
Waterproofing membrane failure suspected but not proven
A builder and an owner disagreeing on the cause of a failure
method: Documentation review against the constructed condition where drawings are available
Targeted water testing of the suspected entry path, including hose and spray testing of facade elements
Intrusive openings at agreed locations to reveal concealed construction detail
Moisture mapping to define the extent of resulting damage
Determination of failure mechanism and its origin in design, materials or workmanship
deliverables: Documented failure mechanism with the evidence chain that establishes it
Photographic and measured record of intrusive findings
Attribution of cause to design, materials or workmanship where the evidence supports it
Targeted rectification strategy rather than speculative repair
Report structured to support insurance, warranty or dispute proceedings
standards: Water testing of facade and waterproofing elements
NCC and relevant Australian Standards as applicable

title: Timber Floor Moisture Investigation & Drying
short: Determine why a floor cupped, buckled or gapped, and whether it can be dried rather than replaced.
headline: A floor that failed usually tells you exactly what happened to it, if you read it properly.
intro: Timber floor failures get replaced when they could often have been dried, and get dried when the subfloor moisture source is still active and will fail them again. This investigation establishes moisture content through the floor system and the subfloor beneath it, determines the source, and gives a defensible answer on whether the floor is recoverable.
signs: Cupping, crowning, buckling or peaking in a timber or engineered floor
Excessive gapping between boards, seasonal or permanent
A new floor failing within its warranty period
A dispute between an installer, a supplier and an owner over cause
Water damage to a floor where replacement has been proposed without drying being attempted
method: Moisture content readings through the floor covering, underlay and subfloor
Subfloor and slab moisture assessment, including relative humidity in slab where relevant
Ambient condition monitoring to establish the service environment the floor sits in
Assessment against manufacturer installation tolerances and acclimatisation requirements
Determination of whether structured drying is viable or replacement is warranted
deliverables: Measured moisture profile through the floor system and substrate
Cause determination covering installation, substrate moisture, service conditions or water event
Viability assessment for drying versus replacement, with reasoning
Drying strategy and target readings where recovery is viable
Report suitable for warranty, insurance or supplier dispute
standards: Calibrated timber and substrate moisture metering

title: Air Leakage & Building Envelope Assessment
short: Locate where the building envelope is losing air, and what that leakage is doing to comfort, energy and moisture.
headline: Uncontrolled air movement carries more moisture into a wall than vapour diffusion ever will.
intro: Air leakage is treated as an energy problem and is often a moisture problem first. Air moving through a gap in the envelope carries water vapour with it, and where that air reaches a cold surface inside the assembly the moisture is deposited there. This assessment locates the leakage paths and evaluates what they mean for comfort, running cost and condensation risk.
signs: Draughts, cold spots or rooms that will not hold temperature
Heating and cooling costs disproportionate to the building size
Mould or damp appearing at junctions, penetrations and service entries
A new or retrofitted building not performing as its design predicted
Verification required for an airtightness target on a performance project
method: Building pressurisation testing to quantify the air change rate of the envelope
Thermal imaging under pressure differential to reveal leakage paths
Smoke tracing at suspected junctions, penetrations and service entries
Assessment of leakage paths against condensation risk, not energy alone
Prioritisation of sealing works by measured impact
deliverables: Quantified air change rate for the tested envelope
Located and photographed leakage paths, ranked by significance
Assessment of moisture risk carried by the identified leakage
Prioritised sealing scope with the reasoning for the order
Verification retest option to confirm the works achieved the target

title: Major Loss & Historical Building Assessment
short: Independent building science assessment for large, complex and heritage losses where the scope is contested.
headline: On a large loss the argument is almost never about whether there was damage.
intro: Major losses turn on scope: how far the damage extends, what is recoverable, what is pre-existing and what the event actually caused. Heritage and historical buildings add a further constraint, because standard drying and demolition approaches can destroy fabric that cannot be replaced. This assessment provides the independent building science position that scope negotiations are settled against.
signs: A large or multi-storey loss where affected extent is disputed
Pre-existing damp or defect complicating attribution of the current event
A heritage or historically significant building requiring a conservation-compatible approach
Multiple parties, insurers or lots requiring one independent position
A restoration scope that appears disproportionate to the event, in either direction
method: Full-building moisture mapping across all affected and adjacent areas and levels
Separation of event-related damage from pre-existing condition, with the evidence for each
Assessment of fabric sensitivity for heritage and historical construction
Drying strategy compatible with the materials present, including traditional fabric
Independent review of proposed restoration scope against measured findings
deliverables: Building-wide measured record of affected extent across all levels
Attribution separating event damage from pre-existing condition
Conservation-compatible drying and rectification strategy where fabric is sensitive
Independent scope position for negotiation between parties
Ongoing monitoring and verification through the drying programme
